items.title: Trump unveils new tariffs over excess industrial capacity, undeterred by midterms defeat
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 25 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump fired a new tariff salvo on Wednesday on 14 major trading partners including China, Japan and the European Union, undeterred in his protectionist push by the losses his Republican Party suffered in US midterm elections.

His administration proposed new maximum potential rates of 20% to 40% to counter excess industrial capacity that it says these countries are promoting. But the US Trade Representative's office said it intends to cap new tariffs at lower levels agreed under trade deals that are completed or still under negotiation.

In unveiling the results of an eight-month unfair trade practices investigation into excess industrial capacity, USTR aims to more fully rebuild Trump's tariff leverage after the Supreme Court in February struck down his broad global duties under a national emergencies law.

The effort also seeks to put Trump's tariffs and associated trade agreements on more solid legal and political grounds by backing them with a court-tested trade law, Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, and addressing foreign subsidies and industrial policies that are viewed as major trade problems by both Republicans and Democrats.

Separately, USTR proposed a new 10% tariff on imports of Brazil's finished Embraer commercial aircraft, and an increase in duties on imports of Brazilian sugar that exceed quotas as part of an effort to push Brasilia to rectify alleged unfair trade practices.

The products were previously exempted from Trump's 25% tariffs on Brazilian goods that were imposed in July under a separate Section 301 investigation. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said he decided to propose the tariff increases after months of talks between the US and Brazil made "no meaningful progress."

CHINA TOPS EXCESS CAPACITY RATES

Under the excess factory capacity probe, USTR said China would face the highest capped rate of 20%, which would be added to duties of roughly 25% imposed during Trump's first term.

That rate would comply with a US-China trade truce that expires on January 10. But if the truce unravels, China's rate would rise to 40%, the USTR said.

Vietnam would face a capped tariff rate of 20% if it reaches a trade agreement with Washington, rising to 35% if negotiations fail.

Greer said the tariffs, which would not take effect until after a January 25 public hearing, were intended to counteract "industrial strategies built on targeting manufacturing, wage and labor suppression, financial and other support, non-market economy inputs, and other market-distorting practices" that undermine the US manufacturing base.

The duties would not stack on top of prior tariffs of 10% or 12.5% imposed under a separate US probe into lax enforcement of anti-forced labor laws in 60 economies, nor would they add to sectoral national security duties on steel, aluminum, autos and other goods.

Greer said the proposed tariffs also would not apply to about $30 billion of Chinese imports under consideration for tariff reductions through a bilateral mechanism known as the Board of Trade.

Washington has long accused China of subsidizing industry and flooding global markets with low-cost exports ranging from steel to electric vehicles and solar products.

A spokesperson for China's embassy in Washington rejected allegations that China is a source of excess capacity, but stopped short of threatening retaliation.

"The so-called issue of 'industrial overcapacity' does not really exist and should not be used as a pretext for political manipulation," the spokesperson said, urging the two sides to jointly deliver on agreements between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

LOWER RATES FOR TRADE DEALS

The USTR also proposed capped tariff rates of 18% for imported goods from Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand and Bangladesh, and 15%, including existing "Most Favored Nation" duties, for Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, the EU and Switzerland.

India, which has yet to reach a trade deal with the Trump administration, would face a 17% tariff rate if an agreement is finalized and a 25% rate if talks fail, the USTR said. Singapore would receive a capped tariff rate of 10%.

Greer told CNBC the proposed caps were consistent with trade agreements reached over the past year that also lowered barriers to US exports.

"We're sticking to that in terms of our proposals because we think a lot of these deals we made actually solve a lot of the problems we see in excess capacity or can go toward it," Greer said, adding that the capped rates are no surprise to trading partners.

Mexico and Norway were excluded from the proposals because investigations into their trade practices remain under way, Greer said.

Even so, the prospect of new trade barriers weighed on stock markets on Wednesday amid a renewed selloff in tech stocks. Major US indexes opened down more than 1%, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq composite down more than 3%.

"It is another reminder that while the legal justification for tariffs keeps changing, US protectionism is becoming increasingly difficult to unwind," ING analysts wrote.

MORE SUPPORT, DURABILITY

Trump's tariffs and their impact on rising living costs were a major issue in Democrats' sweeping victory in midterm elections. A Reuters/Ipsos opinion poll conducted after Republicans' midterm losses found 62% of respondents supported efforts by Democrats to repeal them.

US Senator Ron Wyden, an Oregon Democrat who is expected to chair the Senate Finance Committee when the new Congress begins in January, said: "Not even a month after voters rejected his disastrous trade agenda, Trump has decided to yet again increase prices for Americans. As Finance Committee Chair, I will use every tool at my disposal to end Trump's disastrous tariffs."

But that won't be easy, because there is bipartisan support in Congress for countering excess capacity largely centered in China, said Nathaniel Halvorson, a former USTR official who is now a trade partner at Baker Mckenzie.

Undoing the tariffs also could cause some trade deals to collapse, Halvorson said, and Democrats "would have to consider whether they want to undo a settlement that might be working for US interests to some extent."

Reporting by David Lawder and Andrea Shalal, additional reporting by Jasper Ward; Editing by Tomasz Janowski, Mark Potter and Sanjeev Miglani

items.title: For Trump, doubling down on tariffs is about power, not popularity
items.content_html:
PALM BEACH, Florida, Nov 25 (Reuters) - In midterm elections three weeks ago, US voters punished Republicans over an economy and inflation that many said were made worse by tariffs. President Donald Trump is doubling down on them anyway.

The Trump administration on Wednesday announced a new round of tariffs on goods from 14 major trading partners, including China, Japan and the European Union, a seemingly counterintuitive move that reflects both Trump's decades-old belief in tariffs and a new political reality confronting his White House.

With Democrats set to control Congress for the final two years of his presidency, tariffs are taking on added importance as one of the most potent economic tools Trump can wield without lawmakers' approval.

Tariffs are taxes levied on imports, raising costs for consumers. But Trump sees them as a way to wring concessions from foreign leaders, force corporate CEOs to build plants in the US, raise cash for the government and curry favor with blue-collar voters, according to US officials and other people familiar with the president's thinking.

And after a midterm defeat for his party that threatens to sharply constrain his domestic agenda, Trump is eager to demonstrate that he remains capable of driving economic policy and exercising power even as his legislative clout diminishes, the people said.

“This is all because of tariffs,” Trump told CNBC on Monday as he touted new factories being built in the US. But he said the policy could come with costs. “There's going to be always that little headache during this little transition period.”

Some Republicans in Congress were quick to blame the president's tariff policy for the party's stunning midterm losses. Two-thirds of voters said Trump's tariff policies hurt the national economy, compared with 21% who said they had helped and 12% who found no difference, according to exit polls conducted by SSRS on behalf of a consortium of US media outlets. Yale University's Budget Lab estimated earlier this month that tariffs raised US household costs by $900 annually.

The administration nevertheless proposed new tariffs that would increase duties on targeted imports, with maximum rates of 20% to 40%, though completed or pending trade deals would generally limit them to 10% to 20%.

The new policy, which followed an eight-month review of trading partners' practices, revamps a set of tariffs that Trump imposed in 2025 and the Supreme Court struck down as illegal in February.

Trump's chief trade negotiator, Jamieson Greer, made the tariff announcement with little fanfare on the eve of the US Thanksgiving holiday. Trump himself made no public remarks on the new actions, a marked contrast with his “Liberation Day” tariff announcement last year in the White House Rose Garden.

Despite the muted rollout, the market reaction was swift, with the benchmark S&P 500 (.SPX) closing down a quarter of a percentage point on Wednesday.

Trump had also roiled the markets just days earlier with his extraordinary efforts to restore Jensen Huang as CEO of the chipmaker Nvidia (NVDA.O), a surprise move that tested the bounds of presidential intervention in private markets. Stock markets rallied on Huang's return, but have since pared back.

CONCERNS ABOUT AFFORDABILITY

Democrats seized on the tariff announcement, saying Trump was willfully ignoring voters' anger about high costs and inflation, which have also been fueled by Trump's decision to attack Iran, sparking a conflict that has significantly disrupted oil production and shipping. Several Democrats also argued that, by punishing allies, the policy did little to thwart China's aggressive trade practices.

“Republicans have learned nothing,” incoming House Majority Leader Katherine Clark, a Massachusetts Democrat, said on X.

A former senior US trade official who served under Trump said the midterm rout likely moderated the tariff rates proposed, given that stiffer rates could trigger fresh concerns over affordability.

But while the election focused heavily on rising fuel prices and the cost of living, Trump has made reducing the US trade deficit a cornerstone of his administration, arguing that Washington was effectively shipping factory jobs overseas.

“Putting a stop to American workers, farmers, and businesses being ripped off by lopsided trade agreements has been a key foundation of President Trump's Make America Great Again movement,” said White House spokesman Matthew Middleton, adding that the administration would “continue fighting to lower costs.”

Tariffs also have brought a new revenue source to the federal government after Trump's signature 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act cemented lower individual tax rates.

Trump's protectionist policies have drawn support from some blue-collar labor groups that historically backed Democrats, even as some Republicans recoil from an economic tool they view as hostile to free markets.

United Steelworkers International President Roxanne Brown on Wednesday called the administration's actions “long overdue.” The group endorsed Trump's Democratic opponent, Kamala Harris, in 2024.

Republican US Representative Don Bacon of Nebraska, a Trump critic who is retiring from Congress, took a different view. Calling tariffs “a tax on American consumers” and blaming high inflation and lower wage growth for Republicans' losses, he urged lawmakers to reclaim authority over import duties.

Reporting by Trevor Hunnicutt and Andrea Shalal; Additional reporting by David Morgan; Editing by Colleen Jenkins and Edmund Klamann

items.title: Trump's newest order curtailing birthright citizenship is blocked by second judge
items.content_html:
Nov 25 (Reuters) - A second US judge on Wednesday blocked enforcement of President Donald Trump's executive order limiting the number of people eligible for birthright citizenship, which Trump signed after the US Supreme Court rejected his initial effort to impose restrictions.

US District Judge Christopher Cooper in Washington, DC, issued an injunction in a class action lawsuit filed on behalf of children who would be denied citizenship under the August executive order.

The ruling will stymie Trump's efforts to implement a flagship piece of his administration's hardline immigration crackdown. Another federal judge in Maryland in September also blocked Trump's order, and the administration will now need to overturn both decisions in order to ever enforce it.

"The merits in this case are clear-cut," Cooper said. "The Supreme Court has twice confirmed that all children born in this country are US citizens, save only for the small handful who are not subject to US law."

Cody Wofsy, a lawyer at the American Civil Liberties Union who represented the plaintiffs, in a statement said Trump "needs to accept that birthright citizenship is the law of the land."

"Enough is enough," he said. "The Supreme Court has twice rejected efforts to gut birthright citizenship, in 1898 and again earlier this year. Third time is not the charm."

White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis in a statement called the decision "just another ruling from an activist judge appointed by (former President Barack) Obama attempting to thwart President Trump's commonsense agenda." She said Trump's order was "consistent with the holdings and analysis set forth by the Supreme Court."

Trump signed the order at issue after the Supreme Court in June rejected his first effort from 2025 to end birthright citizenship for children whose parents were not American citizens or legal permanent residents, known as green card holders.

The Supreme Court's ruling concluded that Trump's initial order violated the citizenship clause of the US Constitution's 14th Amendment, which confers citizenship on those born in the United States who are "subject to the jurisdiction thereof."

Soon after the Supreme Court's ruling, Trump tried to again restrict birthright citizenship with a new order taking aim at "birth tourism," in which women travel to the United States to give birth so their children can obtain automatic citizenship.

The order also targeted children whose parents work for foreign governments or international organizations but lack diplomatic immunity and those who have a parent who is classified as an "alien enemy."

But Cooper said the Supreme Court had already made clear that "the President cannot carve out new exceptions to birthright citizenship for children born within the United States and subject to its laws."

He said the high court's ruling in June embraced the Supreme Court's earlier 1898 decision in United States v. Wong Kim Ark in which it interpreted the 14th Amendment as recognizing the right to birthright citizenship regardless of the immigration status of a baby's parents.

The preliminary injunction Cooper issued bars the US Department of State, the US Department of Homeland Security, and the Social Security Administration from enforcing Trump's order against any children covered by the class action.

items.title: How the Trump administration determined Jensen Huang is not a national security threat
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 25 (Reuters) - The US Justice Department did not conduct a formal investigation into Jensen Huang before US President Donald Trump pushed for his return as Nvidia chief executive this week, despite active probes into the chipmaker's customers and allegations he conducted an affair with a woman linked to Chinese intelligence, according to three people familiar with the matter.

Instead, Attorney General Todd Blanche concluded that there was no evidence the tech titan had broken any laws based on the Justice Department's ongoing investigations into two Nvidia clients, Super Micro Computer and Megaspeed International, which are suspected of smuggling advanced microchips to China, said the people, who spoke on condition of anonymity.

That determination, which is subject to change as the probes continue, was crucial to Blanche's decision to tell Trump and Vice President JD Vance over the weekend that he possessed no evidence that Huang posed a risk to national security, said two of the people.

Jensen Huang's reinstatement has angered members of Congress — both Republicans and Democrats — who say it's too soon to set aside questions about whether Nvidia or its CEO endangered US national security. The lack of any additional effort to examine their roles prior to Trump's intervention will likely fuel a push for more investigations on Capitol Hill.

Huang is due to testify next week.

The Justice Department probes of Nvidia customers found no evidence that Huang was acting as an agent of China or knowingly transferred sensitive semiconductor technology or information to China, the two people said. Nvidia was not a target of those investigations and cooperated, providing documents, interviews and other data that helped lead to that conclusion, they added.

There was also no counterintelligence probe of Huang himself. US spy agencies have gathered information on Alice Huang, the former Megaspeed executive and alleged paramour of Jensen Huang suspected of working with Chinese intelligence, said two other people familiar with the effort. But the US had no details that would warrant a probe into the Nvidia CEO, they said.

Counterintelligence investigations are run separately from criminal investigations and are aimed at monitoring and neutralizing national security threats, rather than building a case for indictment.

Justice Department officials concluded that Nvidia and Huang had committed no wrongdoing and did not suspect its chief executive posed a national-security risk, two of the people familiar with the matter said.

Trump and Vance conveyed that conclusion to Nvidia's board, which decided to reinstate Huang, according to Trump's account of events in a CNBC interview on Monday.

Speaking to reporters in Ohio on Wednesday, Vance said Justice Department and national security officials told him that Huang was not the subject of an investigation prior to his reinstatement.

"We were told that he was under no investigation," he said, adding that he didn't think Trump would need to pardon Huang because he had not broken the law. "I haven't seen any evidence again that he committed a crime."

'GOOD CORPORATE CITIZEN'

Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO on November 12 following allegations he conducted affairs with Alice Huang and at least two employees. Jensen Huang acknowledged infidelities but has not confirmed his involvement with Alice Huang specifically. Reuters has been unable to reach her or confirm her links to Chinese spy services.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio briefed Trump in May about the affair, according to the New York Times.

The Times also reported that Alice Huang was in touch with a top Chinese spy official for more than a year during the affair.

Blanche said following Huang's departure that the FBI was "looking into" reports that he was having an affair with a spy, but had not reached any conclusions.

At a press conference on Tuesday, Blanche repeatedly declined to answer questions about how the Trump administration determined that Huang was not a threat to US national security.

He said he had found no evidence that Nvidia engaged in wrongdoing.

"I have no reason to stand up here and say Nvidia is anything other than a good corporate citizen," he said at the press conference.

The Justice Department is also conducting antitrust reviews of Nvidia business deals unrelated to Huang's personal behavior.

A Justice Department spokesperson referred questions to Blanche's statement, and a DOJ official previously told Reuters that no evidence of wrongdoing has been found. The FBI and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence did not respond to requests for comment.

The Wall Street Journal first reported that Blanche's assessment was based on evidence from the two related investigations.

DEFENSIVE BRIEFINGS

Experts said the federal officials bypassed standard counterintelligence protocols.

"No formal Justice Department investigation into the national security allegations has been reported. That's alarming, if unsurprising," said Steve Cash, a former CIA officer who heads The Steady State, an association of former national security officials.

The FBI has provided at least two "defensive briefings" to Nvidia leadership regarding Chinese espionage tactics, according to a law enforcement official familiar with the briefings, who spoke on condition of anonymity.

It was not clear whether those briefings, which have not been previously reported, were standard security engagements routinely provided to major American technology firms, or focused specifically on the threat posed by Alice Huang. It also was not clear whether Huang himself was briefed.

Federal officials often deliver broad warnings to US companies about espionage risks, two former senior law enforcement officials told Reuters.

Defensive briefings can lead to a criminal inquiry if the warnings are ignored, said Kevin Carroll, a former undercover CIA operations officer, but their main purpose is to protect national security.

Reporting by Dan Rosenzweig-Ziff, Erin Banco, Jonathan Landay and Andrew Goudsward; editing by Andy Sullivan, Don Durfee and Nick Zieminski

items.title: New York court upholds Mayor Mamdani's rent freeze
items.content_html:
NEW YORK, Nov 25 (Reuters) - The New York state Supreme Court on Wednesday upheld New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's rent freeze for nearly half of the city's rental units and denied a petition filed by a group of landlords.

Mamdani, who campaigned on promises of affordable housing, called the ruling a "victory for tenants, for affordability and for the principle that working New Yorkers deserve a city they can afford to live in."

The landlords argued that the decision by the Rent Guidelines Board to freeze rents for rent-stabilized apartments, which account for 1 million of the city's 2.3 million rental units, was influenced by Mamdani's loyalists on the board and therefore was not independent. They called it a "sham process" in the complaint.

Justice Brendan Lantry ruled the landlords failed to show that the rent freeze was unreasonable, arbitrary, or capricious and that Mamdani had the right to appoint Rent Guidelines Board members who were on board with his agenda.

"Elections have consequences, a premise that is the backbone of our democracy," the ruling said.

"Mayor Mamdani, a self-proclaimed democratic socialist, was elected Mayor of New York City in the 2025 general election. Upon his election, he appointed members to the Board of his choosing, appointments he was fully empowered to make. That the Board members share his political views and philosophies is of no moment and does not indicate any level of collusion," it added.

The rent freeze applies to rent-stabilized apartments for one-year and two-year leases up for renewal between October 1, 2026, and September 30 next year.

Mamdani said the court's decision will affect more than 2 million people.

"Housing is not a luxury. It is a basic necessity. This holiday weekend, more than 2 million New Yorkers can breathe a little easier," he said in a statement.

items.title: US economy roars ahead in third quarter, inflation remains high in October
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 25 (Reuters) - The US economy grew much faster than initially estimated in the third quarter, while inflation increased further in October, reinforcing expectations that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates next month and again in early 2027.

The sharp upward revision to gross domestic product last quarter, reported by the Commerce Department on Wednesday, marked the quickest economic growth pace in three years. It reflected upgrades to consumer spending and business investment, mostly related to artificial intelligence.

Robust domestic demand is fueling inflation, with a measure of underlying price pressures in October posting its biggest year-over-year increase since late 2023. The economy has powered ahead despite the ongoing US-Israeli war with Iran.

"It is more urgent than ever that Fed officials step up the pace of interest rate hikes to cool off economic demand," said Christopher Rupkey, chief economist at FWDBONDS. "It was once thought that import tariffs and energy prices from the Mideast war were one-off factors behind the higher inflation numbers, but increasingly the inflation fires look to be stoked by old-fashioned economic demand pressures."

GDP increased at a 4.3% annualized rate last quarter, the Commerce Department's Bureau of Economic Analysis said in its second estimate of third-quarter GDP. It was the fastest pace since the third quarter of 2023. The economy was previously estimated to have grown at a 3.4% pace.

Economists polled by Reuters had expected GDP growth to be revised up to a 3.5% pace. The economy grew at a 2.2% rate in the April-June quarter.

Growth in consumer spending, which accounts for more than two-thirds of the economy, was revised up to a 4.2% rate. That was the strongest pace since the fourth quarter of 2024 and was an upgrade from the previously reported 3.8% pace.

Spending is being driven mostly by higher-income households, whose wealth was boosted by the stock market before the ongoing AI-led selloff. Economists expect consumer spending to slow to a still-healthy pace in the fourth quarter, though declining gasoline prices should ease some of the financial pressure on middle- and lower-income households.

Average retail gasoline prices have dropped below $4 a gallon for the first time since mid-July, data from the US Energy Information Administration showed.

Disposable household income, adjusted for taxes and inflation, rebounded in October, and the saving rate increased after declining for two straight months, the BEA said in another report. Low layoffs, with first-time claims for state unemployment benefits at a 57-year low, are also expected to help underpin spending.

But some of the relief at the gasoline pump could be offset by higher prices elsewhere after President Donald Trump on Wednesday fired a new tariff salvo against 14 major trading partners, including China, Japan and the European Union.

Business spending on equipment increased at a 21.8% rate in the third quarter, the fastest since the third quarter of 2020. That figure was an upgrade from the 20.9% rate of growth estimated last month. Business investment has posted three straight quarters of double-digit growth, and momentum appeared to have persisted early in the fourth quarter.

A third report from the Commerce Department's Census Bureau showed non-defense capital goods orders excluding aircraft, a proxy for business spending, jumped 1.2% in October after rising 0.8% in September. Shipments of these so-called core capital goods, which go into the calculation of the business equipment spending component in the GDP report, rose 0.6% last month after advancing 1.3% in September.

GROWING QUESTIONS OVER AI FUNDING

A cloud, however, is hanging over AI. Broader questions about AI funding, profitability, regulation and public resistance to data-center developments have emerged and persist even after the surprise reinstatement of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Tech firms have borrowed huge sums over the past year for AI spending. AI remains a key pillar of the economy.

An AI-related investment slowdown could reduce imports, which subtracted 2.58 percentage points from GDP growth last quarter.

"The tech selloff, while probably not putting any dent in fourth-quarter investment spending, may start to prompt a cooling for later in 2027 as funding comes under a little more pressure," said James Knightley, chief international economist at ING. "Cooler tech investment growth would mean less of a drag from net trade, so it wouldn't be a disaster."

Final sales to private domestic purchasers, which exclude inventories, trade and government, accelerated at a 5.8% rate in the third quarter, the fastest pace since the second quarter of 2021, the GDP report showed. This measure of domestic demand, closely watched by policymakers, was previously estimated to have surged at a 4.9% rate.

The Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index increased 0.3% in October after gaining 0.5% in September, the BEA said. PCE inflation was lifted by higher prices for goods, including food and household furnishings, as well as services such as recreation, dining out and hotel stays. In the 12 months through October, PCE inflation increased 3.8% after advancing 3.6% in September.

Excluding the volatile food and energy components, the PCE Price Index increased 0.3% for the third straight month. So-called core PCE inflation increased 3.3% on a year-over-year basis in October, the largest advance since November 2023, after climbing 3.1% in September.

The Fed tracks the PCE price measures for its 2% inflation target. Financial markets have priced in a quarter-percentage-point rate hike at the US central bank's December 8-9 meeting from the current 3.75%-4.00% range, and are expecting another increase in January, CME Group's FedWatch tool showed.

Fed Governor Christopher Waller has signaled he could support a bigger half-percentage-point rate increase to quell inflation. Economists, however, said tightening financial market conditions amid an equities selloff had reduced the need for such an aggressive move.

Stocks on Wall Street extended their decline on Wednesday, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite and blue-chip S&P 500 indexes on track for their worst November since 2008. The dollar slipped against a basket of currencies. US Treasury yields fell.

Despite the recent pullback in oil prices, economists expect inflation to remain elevated in 2027, pointing to the still-volatile Middle East situation and the lack of clarity on the implementation of the latest round of tariffs.

"The more important decision is whether the direction of inflation on top of a broadening out of price increases will necessitate consecutive increases in January and March of next year despite the sizeable declines in oil, gasoline and diesel prices in November," said Joseph Brusuelas, chief economist at RSM. "Based on the totality of the data, that answer today would likely be yes."

Reporting by Lucia Mutikani; Editing by Chizu Nomiyama and Paul Simao

items.title: US Army declares success in detonation of lead-based explosives stockpile in Iowa
items.content_html:
MIDDLETOWN, Iowa, Nov 25 (Reuters) - The US Army conducted a controlled detonation of an aging stockpile of lead-based explosives in rural Iowa on Wednesday, declaring the operation a success at safely destroying the unstable material while minimizing toxic fallout.

Residents of the Iowa farm town of Middletown closest to the adjacent munitions depot were evacuated ahead of time as a precaution, while others hunkered down inside their homes to avoid exposure to lead dust emitted from the blast.

The Army and the US Environmental Protection Agency said emission monitors detected zero levels of airborne lead in the surrounding region immediately after the explosion. Still, residents were told to remain indoors until officials gave the all-clear, and some expressed doubts about official reassurances.

The detonation followed days of public rancor and legal wrangling over the controversial disposal plan, which authorities said was far safer than waiting for the deteriorating chemical drums to eventually blow up on their own.

Shortly after 9 a.m. CST (1500 GMT), the Federal Emergency Management Agency posted a message on its X account confirming the detonation had been carried out and urging nearby residents to remain indoors for the time being.

"Following this morning's controlled detonation in Middletown, Iowa, residents within 20 miles who have not evacuated should continue to shelter in place and follow @EPA safety guidance until given the all clear by officials. FEMA has provided safe lodging to those who evacuated," the agency wrote.

A short time later, acting Army Secretary Adam Telle declared that the "controlled, mitigated detonation," designed to dispose of nearly 5 tons (4,500 kg) of highly volatile lead azide stored in 68 degrading plastic barrels, had "exceeded all expectations and was a huge success."

"The threat of a spontaneous detonation has been eliminated," he said on X.

'NO KICKOUT'

In a videotaped public service message posted online afterward, Army Colonel Aaron Teller, a munitions specialist who oversaw the operation, said the demolition and the array of safety measures to muffle the blast and emissions worked.

"All of the lead azide barrels were definitively removed," Teller said, adding there were no secondary explosions.

"There was no kickout. There was no infrastructure damage in or around our installation," Teller said. "We reduced as close to zero as is absolutely humanly possible the risk to the health and safety of the people of Middletown and the extended communities throughout Iowa."

In a local television feed from the site, recorded from a considerable distance, the sound of an explosion could be heard, and a cloud of gray smoke was seen rising into the dawn-lit sky behind a line of trees before quickly dissipating.

Public safety concerns had focused on expectations that the explosion would spew a plume of toxic lead dust over homes, crops and livestock beyond the detonation site at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, about 150 miles southwest of the state capital Des Moines.

The EPA reported one hour after the blast that "real-time air monitors are reporting zero detection of airborne lead throughout the region." The agency said it would continue taking air, soil and water samples throughout the day to compare with more than 1,200 samples collected the day before the blast.

Residents in the area expressed relief mixed with skepticism about the government's candor regarding emissions from the exploded chemicals.

"If you're going to blow them up, there are going to be some particles," said Rhonda Woodson, a former employee of the ammunition plant who lives in nearby Burlington, Iowa.

Woodson said she thought the detonation may have been "too hyped up" but also said she did not fully trust information coming from the federal government.

Still, Woodson's neighborhood appeared deserted some three hours after the blast. "I see no animals, no kids. Nobody's outside," she said.

CONTAINMENT MEASURES

Government experts had stressed that the controlled detonation of the chemical stockpile was the safest way of disposing of it. The toxic material, growing ever more unstable with the arrival of colder weather, was otherwise certain to eventually explode on its own, they said. Experts likewise concluded that attempting to chemically neutralize or relocate the storage drums would have triggered an uncontrolled blast.

Army projections released on Tuesday had shown that lead dust could settle on surfaces as far as 40 miles southwest of the blast site, extending through southeastern Iowa into northern Missouri. Airborne particles could travel nearly 100 miles within eight hours, according to projections.

US and Iowa agriculture officials estimated that 350 farms might be impacted by lead fallout, based on pre-detonation forecasts.

On Wednesday, officials said various containment structures and equipment put in place at the site had evidently worked to minimize the amount of lead particulates belched from the detonation.

Those measures included earthen berms along with two towering walls stacked with tanks of water for release into the blast zone. A misting apparatus also was employed to dampen the surrounding terrain, and fire trucks flooded the blast site with aqueous foam.

Lead azide has long been used as the chief detonating material in military ordnance. The explosive chemical was deemed largely obsolete years ago, and the Army brought unused stockpiles from bases around the country to Iowa in 2009.

The crisis in Middletown started after an inspection in March discovered a dangerous crystallization of the storage drums and material in them, a sign that it had become dangerously unstable.

(This story has been corrected to fix the Army official's title and first name to acting Army Secretary Adam Telle, in paragraph 7.)

items.title: 'I'm going to drive': FAA outage and high fares reshape Thanksgiving travel plans
items.content_html:
NEW YORK, Nov 25 (Reuters) - Dinese Jackson couldn't stomach spending roughly $1,500 to fly herself and her two children from Raleigh, North Carolina, to Dallas, Texas, for Thanksgiving, more than double what she had paid for similar trips in the past.

Still, she kept checking airfares in hopes they would drop, until the Federal Aviation Administration's nationwide ground stop on November 13 cemented her decision to make the trip by car instead, even at the price of a 17-hour drive.

"When that happened on Friday, I was like, 'Yep, I'm keeping my car reservation. I'm going to go ahead and drive for sure," the 51-year-old credit analyst said. "For those that are flying, I just think it's going to be chaos."

A router outage on November 13 caused a communications failure at air traffic control centers and triggered a nearly five-hour nationwide disruption impacting more than 18,000 flights and affecting about 1 million passengers.

Just a few days later, travelers faced fresh disruptions when United Airlines (UAL.O) suffered a widespread technology outage and Delta Air Lines' (DAL.N) automated weight-and-balance system failed on Sunday, delaying more than 2,000 flights nationwide, shaking confidence in air travel ahead of the Thanksgiving travel rush.

The rising cost of airfare, which has hit 10-year highs for the holiday period, had already persuaded some Americans to stay home this year. Airlines for America forecast nearly 29 million passengers will travel between November 20 and 30, down from last year's forecast of 31 million passengers.

HIGHEST AIRFARE IN A DECADE

Two weeks before Thanksgiving, domestic airfares for the holiday travel period averaged about $469 in 2026, about a 57% year-over-year increase, according to data from travel search engine, Kayak. Travel booking app Hopper said months of elevated jet fuel costs due to the conflict in Iran have helped push Thanksgiving and Christmas fares to 10-year highs.

United Airlines (UAL.O) said it expects more than 6.6 million customers over a 12-day period, on par with last year. American Airlines (AAL.O) said it plans to welcome 8 million travelers in the same period, and plans to operate 4% more flights than in 2025. US airlines are operating 2% more flights on average this Thanksgiving than last year, while seat capacity is up 1%, Cirium, a flight analytics company, said.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Wednesday that airlines operated 52,000 flights on Tuesday, marking the busiest day for U.S. air travel in 16 years.

About 50% of flight delays were due to inclement weather and 24% due to flight volume, he added.

"The rest of the holiday travel week will be challenging," he said noting coastal storms expected to impact the Mid-Atlantic and portions of the Northeast.

Fewer Americans are traveling by air in 2026 as fares rise and disruptions mount. The last time the Transportation Security Administration screened more than 3 million passengers in a single day was November 30, 2025. The TSA has not screened 3 million passengers on any day this year, compared to eight times in 2025.

During the Thanksgiving Holiday, the agency expects to screen about 3% fewer passengers year-on-year.

Jennifer Shaw, 57, was less than thrilled to learn her son planned to forfeit his non-refundable plane ticket home from college in Michigan. Instead, he opted to drive 10 hours to Monmouth County, New Jersey, with friends rather than risk getting stranded at an airport during the holiday rush.

"Even though I might be worried that he's driving 10 hours with a group of boys, at least I don't have to worry about the airlines," Shaw said.

A PAUSE IN UPGRADES

FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said last week the agency was "very close" to being able to disclose the root cause of the router outage. The FAA declined to say Monday when it plans to offer an update.

On November 17, the FAA said it had immediately paused deployment of additional routers.

"I'm hoping the government is not going to do any more upgrades during this time that we're going to be away," said retiree Liz Dougherty, 63, who plans to fly from North Carolina to Spain to take a cruise for the holiday, adding that the November 13 flight halt was "definitely in the back of my mind."

About 81.5 million Americans will travel at least 50 miles for Thanksgiving over a six-day period, according to AAA estimates, down only slightly from last year's total of 81.6 million. However, more Americans are expected to take cruises, buses, and trains to their destinations.

Bus and travel search engine, Wanderu, said the ground stop gave the company its busiest day of the year so far, with bookings made that Friday up about 16% from last year. Bus operator Flix North America said bookings for Thanksgiving are up 17% from last year.

Amtrak said the company is again expecting a record in 2026 after 1.2 million customer trips during last year's Thanksgiving holiday.

Reporting by Doyinsola Oladipo in New York, additional reporting by David Shepardson in Washington; Editing by Christian Plumb, Aurora Ellis and Nick Zieminski

items.title: US CDC reports nine measles-related deaths in 2026
items.content_html:
Nov 25 (Reuters) - The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported nine measles-related deaths in the United States this year, as the country battles its worst outbreak of the highly contagious viral infection in decades.

The US had recorded 6,039 confirmed measles cases as of November 24, across 47 jurisdictions, according to the agency's website on Wednesday. That includes 18 cases among international visitors.

The CDC updated its tally after the National Center for Health Statistics received additional reports from states and verified that the deaths had occurred and that measles was the underlying cause, a Department of Health and Human Services spokesperson said.

Based on publicly reported state figures, however, the US has recorded at least 14 measles-associated deaths this year, including nine fatalities in Pennsylvania, three in Wisconsin and one each in Virginia and New York state.

A discrepancy between state and federal death tallies arose earlier this year after CDC, under US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., began using National Center for Health Statistics mortality data instead of state figures.

"The discrepancy between state and federal measles-related death figures is concerning and risks confusing the public about the true toll of this outbreak," said Frederic Bertley, immunologist and CEO of the Center of Science and Industry.

"Regardless of the precise number, these deaths are alarming and reflect the consequences of declining vaccination coverage," Bertley said.

Cases in the US have reached a 35-year high, a resurgence driven largely by unvaccinated people that this month stripped the country of its hard-fought measles elimination status.

CDC data showed that 671 patients, or 11% of confirmed cases, were hospitalized, with children aged under 5 years recording the highest hospitalization rate at 17%. The agency also said the death count could change as it reviews additional information.

On Wednesday, Pennsylvania, the hardest-hit US state, reported 1,679 measles cases so far this year, including 87 new cases over the past seven days and 340 hospitalizations.

Reporting by Kunal Das in Bengaluru; Editing by Diti Pujara and Shilpi Majumdar

items.title: What to know about US Army's detonation of lead azide in Iowa
items.content_html:
November 25 - The US Army said it destroyed 68 barrels, or nearly 10,000 pounds (4,536 kg), of a deteriorating lead compound used in explosives, in a controlled detonation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, on Wednesday.

The detonation took place after a week of public outcry and legal wrangling. Many worried that the explosion could release a plume of toxic lead dust over homes, crops and livestock far beyond the detonation site.

Here is what you need to know:

WHAT IS LEAD AZIDE?

Lead azide is an explosive chemical that was used to detonate military munitions but is now largely obsolete.

On Tuesday, US officials said in a news conference that stockpiles from military bases around the country had been moved to the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in 2009 for long-term storage.

WHY DID THE ARMY DETONATE THE LEAD AZIDE?

The Army said that in March it discovered the lead azide stockpile had undergone crystallization. This made the stockpile unstable, officials said, and certain to eventually explode. They said they concluded that attempting to chemically neutralize or relocate the storage drums would have triggered an uncontrolled blast.

WHAT ARE THE RISKS?

Patrick O'Shaughnessy, a public health professor at the University of Iowa, said immediate risks from inhaling lead particles would likely be mitigated if people sheltered from the dust plume as it passed over them.

Longer-term risks come from lead dust settling on homes, farms and in the environment, where it will not break down further.

Exposure to lead dust can cause wide-ranging health problems in humans and animals, O'Shaughnessy said. Children in particular are at risk because lead can inhibit the development of the brain and its cognitive abilities.

The Iowa Department of Health and Human Services recommended that residents in affected areas keep windows and doors closed for 24–48 hours after the detonation and shut off heating and cooling systems that bring in outside air.

It said residents should clean surfaces in potentially affected areas after the detonation and consult healthcare providers about blood testing for lead.

In a Tuesday briefing, Sean Kaufman, an official with the US Department of Health and Human Services, said pregnant women, children and people with chronic diseases "definitely want to be out of" affected areas.

WHO WILL BE AFFECTED?

Hours before the blast on Wednesday, the Army released projections showing lead dust from the plume could settle on surfaces as far as 40 miles (64 km) southwest of the blast site, extending through southeastern Iowa into northern Missouri. Airborne particles could travel nearly 100 miles within eight hours, according to projections.

The EPA said in a statement after the detonation that its air monitors were reporting zero detection of airborne lead throughout the region.

"Over the course of the upcoming minutes, hours, and days, EPA's 300 employees and contractors, who have been pre-positioned on the ground, will be conducting extensive and thorough monitoring, taking samples of air, land, and water, and deploying remediation efforts if necessary," said EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin.

Some residents who spoke to Reuters said they had gathered their own soil samples to be tested independently.

WAS THE DETONATION SUCCESSFUL?

In a videotaped public service message posted online afterward, Army Colonel Aaron Teller, a munitions specialist who oversaw the operation, said the demolition worked, as did the safety measures to muffle the blast and limit emissions.

"All of the lead azide barrels were definitively removed," Teller said.

IS THIS UNUSUAL?

Teller said the last detonation of a large amount of lead azide was in 1977. That year, 7,000 pounds (3,175 kg) of the chemical were detonated in Colorado in the open air with no mitigation, yet 75% of the lead particulate was contained, he said, but gave no other details.

Reporting by Renee Hickman; editing by Donna Bryson and David Gregorio

items.title: US judge blocks FCC from threatening Disney-owned ABC stations
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 25 (Reuters) - A US judge on Wednesday barred the Federal Communications Commission from revoking Walt Disney's (DIS.N) licenses for its eight company-owned ABC TV stations, in a dramatic blow to President Donald Trump's efforts to rein in American media companies.

"This is not a close case," US District Judge Loren Alikhan wrote. ABC has a "weighty interest in 'vindicating their right to be free of retaliation for (their) protected speech,'" the judge wrote in a case that was a key test of the free-speech rights of media outlets.

The judge said the FCC appears to be carrying out a retaliatory campaign driven by Trump.

FCC Chair Brendan Carr, who was tapped to lead the agency in January 2025, "has taken President Trump's rhetoric as his marching orders," the judge added.

Trump has repeatedly urged broadcasters to drop comedy or news programs that he dislikes or which have been critical of him or his administration. He has also pressed the FCC on a number of occasions to revoke ABC's licenses.

Carr, the White House, Disney and ABC did not immediately respond to requests for comment late on Wednesday.

Disney and ABC sued the FCC in August to block an unprecedented early review of licenses for eight ABC stations, arguing that the Trump administration was trying to punish the network over its broadcast content.

Carr ordered the reviews in April, even though the stations' license renewals were not scheduled to be considered before October 2028. The FCC had not ordered an early review in more than 50 years before April.

The reviews were ordered in April, a day after Trump urged ABC to fire late-night host Jimmy Kimmel.

Broadcast stations need FCC licenses to use public airwaves. While license revocations are extremely rare, critics say the threat of losing a license can pressure broadcasters and raise concerns about government interference in editorial and programming decisions. Networks have broad free-speech protections over programming choices.

Trump has waged an aggressive series of attacks on the news media and the latest move follows a two-year-long battle between Trump and Disney. In July, Trump again called for ABC stations to lose their licenses because the network refused to air a prime-time speech on elections.

The FCC is also investigating ABC daytime talk show "The View," which discusses US politics, after saying it may be subject to federal rules requiring broadcasters to provide equal-time opportunities to political candidates.

Disney noted earlier that as a result, the program did not invite any political candidates to appear ahead of the November midterm elections, citing the FCC's "pressure campaign."

Trump has also been more broadly criticized by free-speech advocates for attempting to target critics, deport foreign student protesters and freeze federal funds for educational institutions. His efforts have faced legal challenges and some judicial setbacks.

Reporting by David Shepardson and Kanishka Singh in Washington; Editing by Ryan Patrick Jones and Thomas Derpinghaus

items.title: EXCLUSIVE: US famine monitor to halt reporting as funding shortfall hits staff, sources say
items.content_html:
NAIROBI, Nov 25 (Reuters) - More than half the field workers at the US government's famine monitor will lose their jobs by the end of the year due to a lack of funding, six people told Reuters, leaving it unable to help fend off famines made more likely by El Nino and aid cuts.

December 1 30-day termination notices to dozens of employees of the Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS NET) mean it will be unable to produce its next food security update, three of the people, all with direct knowledge of the issue, said.

An email from the monitor to aid officials sent on Tuesday and seen by Reuters said the December update would not be published because the US State Department had not confirmed funding for the fiscal year that began in October, forcing staff to "initiate contingency closeout actions".

The update is crucial for countries on the brink of famine such as Sudan, Yemen, South Sudan and Somalia, since it was expected to include details of the areas hit hardest by drastic food shortages. Early indications of a famine help humanitarian agencies and policymakers assess and deploy lifesaving relief measures to prevent further deaths from hunger.

"We will endeavor to remain as engaged as possible during this period of disruption and anticipate that we will soon be able to confirm funding and restart full operations," the email said.

The anticipated terminations and the fact that the December report - one of three such updates produced in a year - will not be published have not been reported before. The people Reuters spoke to said they had no details of how and when funding and reporting might resume or whether any jobs might be reinstated.

A spokesperson for FEWS NET asked Reuters to direct all questions regarding its funding to the State Department.

MONTHS OF UNCERTAINTY

Washington-based FEWS NET is one of just two global hunger monitors — the other being the UN-backed Integrated Food Security Phase Classification or IPC — and works in more than 30 countries.

Around 200 people of many different nationalities, most of them field staff based in regional hubs or country offices, work on data collection and analysis for FEWS NET. Additional staff run the website and information storage.

In October, termination notices had already been sent to 20% of FEWS NET staff following months of uncertainty about the monitor's financial future, the six people said.

Four of the people said staff at the hunger monitor warned the State Department as recently as last week that its operations would have to cease without financial guarantees. An internal email dated July 24 and seen by Reuters ordered a pause on travel and recruitment, citing a cash crunch.

In the past, funding for the hunger monitor, which was part of the now shuttered US Agency for International Development, would have been approved before the fiscal year began on October 1, the people said.

They added they did not know whether the lack of funding was due to internal bottlenecks and poor management or if it reflected a deliberate decision by the Trump administration to downsize or close FEWS NET.

The State Department did not respond immediately to questions from Reuters about the future of FEWS NET or the reasons for the lack of funding.

CONTRACTOR DRAWS UP CLOSEOUT PLAN

Aid workers have struggled to respond to surging needs after widespread funding cuts by governments including the United States, long the world's largest donor, forced organisations to cut their workforce and operations.

The spending for FEWS NET's field operations is channelled through private contractor Chemonics, which traditionally pays the monitor's expenses upfront before being reimbursed by the US government.

The six people said that Chemonics has continued to cover FEWS NET expenses for months while it awaited funding approval from the State Department. The contractor sent a closeout plan to the State Department earlier this month, with a view to winding down operations, they said.

Chemonics did not respond immediately to a request for comment.

QUESTIONS FROM CONGRESS

The monitor, which aims to forecast hunger crises six to 12 months in advance, was established in 1985 following a deadly famine in Ethiopia that shocked the world and highlighted the need for early warning systems.

Since beginning operations during former President Ronald Reagan's second term, it had received bipartisan support until last year, when the shutdown of USAID took it offline for five months. It resumed work in late June last year.

Earlier this year, the State Department ordered the monitor to stop publishing reports about crisis-hit Somalia, Yemen and Afghanistan, without offering any explanation, according to the July 24 internal email seen by Reuters.

The suspension of the reports, lifted in September, prompted criticism from Gregory Meeks, the top-ranking Democrat on the House of Representatives' Foreign Affairs Committee.

Meeks told Reuters that the State Department was putting "millions of lives at risk as it delays funding for FEWS NET".

"The Department should stop stalling and allow FEWS NET to do what it does best — provide analysis to prevent famine abroad," he said.

The State Department did not respond to a request for comment on the remarks by Meeks.

items.title: Nvidia faces questions from top Senate antitrust Democrat
items.content_html:
Nov 25 (Reuters) - US Senator Cory Booker, a New Jersey Democrat, demanded answers from Nvidia on Wednesday about CEO Jensen Huang's return, according to a letter seen by Reuters, indicating the chipmaker's market power will be a likely focus of antitrust scrutiny by Democrats.

Booker's request adds to congressional scrutiny of Huang's return and Nvidia's business links to China. Booker is the top Democrat on the Senate antitrust subcommittee and likely to lead it when the next Congress begins in January. Tech companies are expected to face scrutiny as part of a larger wave of Democratic investigations.

Booker asked for information about the Trump administration's communications with Nvidia's board leading up to Huang's resignation and reinstatement, including President Donald Trump's assurances that Huang posed no national security threat.

Nvidia must also preserve board records on the decision and details of its independent investigation on the company's compliance with US export controls, he said in the letter to Nvidia Chair Harvey Jones, dated Wednesday.

Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Huang resigned as head of one of the world's most valuable companies on November 12 amid reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman alleged to have spied for China. Nvidia reinstated Huang on Monday after Trump called for his return.

The incident roiled stock markets, sending technology stocks sliding and then, when Huang was reinstated, pushing Nvidia (NVDA.O) shares up more than 31%. The stock was down 8% in early US trading on Wednesday.

MARKET POWER QUESTIONS

Booker said Trump's involvement in Huang's reinstatement and the resulting stock market surge raise questions about Nvidia's market power and whether the company is "too big to hold accountable."

"The antitrust laws exist to prevent this kind of concentration where a company is so dominant that a mere change in its leadership threatens household savings and the broader economy," Booker wrote.

Lawmakers swiftly criticized Huang's reinstatement and launched probes. Huang is expected to appear before the House intelligence committee in a closed-door session on December 1 and at a public hearing of the Senate banking committee on December 3.

The antitrust subcommittee has jurisdiction to probe Nvidia's "apparent dominance that has led the federal government to treat its leadership as indispensable to the economy," Booker said in the letter.

items.title: US grocers serve up Thanksgiving deals even as turkey prices climb
items.content_html:
NEW YORK/CHICAGO, Nov 25 (Reuters) - Major US retailers including Walmart (WMT.O) are offering Thanksgiving meal kits at or below last year's prices to woo shoppers weary of inflation. But the grocers face an inconvenient truth: wholesale prices for turkey and potatoes, the holiday's two marquee staples, have jumped since last year, forcing them to eat some extra costs.

Their hope is that, once inside, shoppers are indulging in drinks, snacks and desserts, industry analysts say.

"Turkey and other highly visible Thanksgiving staples are important price signals for shoppers," said Sally Lyons Wyatt, consumer packaged goods lead at research firm Circana. "Retailers have an incentive to promote aggressively or absorb some cost pressure to reinforce the value of the overall meal."

This month, when voters roundly punished US President Donald Trump's Republican Party in the US midterm elections, affordability emerged as a top concern, exit polls showed.

Wholesale price assessments for frozen tom turkeys were up 12% from a year earlier at a record high of $2 per pound as of November 9, according to commodity data firm Expana.

Yet retailers are holding the line: in the four weeks to November 7, whole-bird turkeys from the frozen section were 6.3% less per pound than in the same period last year, data from NielsenIQ showed. For russet potatoes, wholesale prices soared about 46%, Expana found — yet in retail stores, a 3-pound bag cost just 2.9% more year-over-year, the NielsenIQ data revealed.

Last year, as tariffs roiled global markets, Trump pointed to Walmart's generously discounted $40 Thanksgiving deal as evidence that prices were under control.

This year, with inflation and gas prices shrinking shoppers' wallets, Walmart is going even lower. The US giant unveiled a 26-item, $35 Thanksgiving meal kit that can feed 10 people, with turkeys ranging from 10 to 16 pounds. It's $5 cheaper than last year's, with four extra items.

Not to be outdone, German discount grocer Lidl announced a 10-person Thanksgiving package featuring 29 items and a 14-pound turkey, for $33.56. Lidl, which had initially set the price $2 higher, moved it gradually lower in November, promising on its website it "will not be beaten ... by Walmart."

Michael Swanson, chief agricultural economist at Wells Fargo, called these approaches loss-leading strategies, aimed at using discounts on popular items to lure shoppers. Once in the store, "you also load up on chocolates and sweets ... and suddenly you'll be spending quite a bit of money," Swanson said.

MANAGING COSTS

Even though aggressive meal deals can eat into profit margins, grocers can offset at least a portion of added costs by including products in kits that have become cheaper at wholesale, said Alexis Villacis, an agricultural economist at Ohio State University.

For example, wholesale ham prices had fallen 32% year over year as of October, Expana found. But according to NielsenIQ, families that eschew turkey for a whole ham on Thanksgiving were paying only 15.5% less per pound in the four weeks ended November 7.

Major retailers can also protect margins by negotiating favorable deals with suppliers. "Retailers like Kroger (KR.N) and Walmart, they have the upper hand," Villacis said. "If they want to push the turkey industry to give them discounts, they have the power to do so."

However, both suppliers and grocers were bound to absorb some incremental costs for rising input costs, such as diesel fuel: "If consumers pay similar prices as last year, and you have input costs that are higher, the costs have to be absorbed somewhere," said Scott Vinson, an executive vice president of turkey company Butterball.

DEVIL IS IN THE DETAILS

At low-priced German-owned chain Aldi, a $39, 10-person dinner is a tick more affordable than last year's $40 deal but includes just 15 items versus 26 last year. It does not include russet potatoes.

Aldi Chief Commercial Officer Scott Patton attributed the smaller basket to Aldi's decision to build the meal around an annual American Farm Bureau Federation benchmark tracking the cost of a classic Thanksgiving meal. Comparing this year to last, Patton said, "isn't apples-to-apples and doesn't reflect the value we're delivering."

The Farm Bureau pegged the average cost of Thanksgiving dinner for 10 people at $58.63, up 6% from last year. It said the cost of a 16-pound turkey jumped about 10% to $1.48 per pound, but shoppers found deals for as low as 69 cents per pound.

Wells Fargo forecast the average 10-person Thanksgiving meal to cost $79 this year. That is more than double what the value retailers are charging, yet still less than $8 per person — quite modest for a multi-course culinary bonanza, Swanson said.

If the race to cut prices leads to a drop in quality, it could backfire: "People are open to trade-offs," Swanson said. "They're not open to rip-offs."

Reporting by Nicholas P. Brown in New York and Tom Polansek in Chicago. Editing by Lisa Jucca and Nick Zieminski

items.title: Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade postponed due to weather for first time in 100 years
items.content_html:
Nov 25 (Reuters) - The 100th edition of the annual Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York City will be postponed for two days until Saturday due to forecasts of a major storm with high winds, marking the first time the event has been rescheduled due to severe weather.

"The safety of our participants and spectators is our top priority, and after close consultation with our city and agency partners, we have made the decision to move this year's celebration," Macy's (M.N) department store chain, which sponsors the event, said in a statement on Wednesday.

The three-hour parade through Manhattan, from 77th Street and Central Park West to Macy's flagship store at Herald Square, is now set to commence at 8:30 a.m. EST (1330 GMT) Saturday, the retailer said.

At an outdoor Thanksgiving-eve news conference, Mayor Zohran Mamdani said the choice to reschedule was coordinated with Macy's, the New York Police Department and other agencies.

"We know that our city is the greatest city in the world, and we also know that in our city nothing comes easily, and you have to plan for every possibility," he said.

Mamdani said gale-force winds forecast for Thursday, a situation that has previously interfered with the safety of the parade's signature balloon displays, were a major factor in the decision to reschedule.

The parade was suspended from 1942 to 1944 during World War Two, but has never been postponed before because of weather conditions.

The annual parade, televised nationwide, has become enmeshed in the traditions of America's Thanksgiving holiday, a spectacle of huge inflatable cartoon characters, marching bands, clowns, cheerleaders and popular music acts performing live. Thousands line the streets of Manhattan to watch.

The National Weather Service has issued a high-wind warning and a coastal flood warning for New York City for Thursday into Friday.

The city was expected to face wind gusts of 50 to 60 miles per hour (80 to 96 kph) on Thursday, with sustained winds of 30 to 38 mph, the city's emergency management office said.

Forecasters said this week that storms bringing heavy rain and winds up and down the US eastern seaboard were threatening to delay flights during one of the busiest travel weeks of the year.

Inclement weather has disrupted the parade before, including the 1997 procession when heavy wind gusts pushed a Cat in the Hat balloon into a lamppost, toppling a section of the street light into a crowd of onlookers below. Two people were hospitalized with head injuries.

Two other large balloons, inflatable likenesses of the Pink Panther and Barney the dinosaur, were also badly damaged in the blustery weather.

In response, then-Mayor Rudy Giuliani formed a task force to review the situation, leading to new size restrictions on the parade balloons and the removal of lampposts along the parade route.

All of the cartoon balloons that were brought into Manhattan and inflated in advance on Wednesday for this year's event must now be deflated and returned to their facility in New Jersey and rendered "parade-ready" all over again, a process that normally takes a week, said Will Coss, head of Macy's Studios.

City officials also are taking security factors into consideration, with an expanded NYPD presence planned along the parade route, despite an absence of any "known specific or credible threats" to the parade, city Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch said.

items.title: US House Democrats expand probe into Trump Jr.'s investments
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 24 (Reuters) - US House Democrats probing Donald Trump Jr.'s business dealings have sought records from prediction market firm Polymarket, vaping company Juul and two other companies tied to 1789 Capital, the venture capital firm where the president's son is a partner.

In letters published on Tuesday, US Representative Jamie Raskin, a Maryland Democrat expected to chair the House Judiciary Committee next year, asked the companies — which also include GrabAGun (PEW.N) and Hadrian Automation — for a range of records of communications with 1789 Capital and its executives.

"The probe examines whether the President's son and his business partners helped steer federal contracts or regulatory decisions to companies in which they had a significant financial interest or used advance knowledge of those forthcoming decisions to make investments and profit," Raskin's office wrote in a press release. Raskin opened the probe in August.

Democrats, who take control of Congress in January, are preparing a flurry of investigations into Republican President Donald Trump and his administration, from contracts and potential conflicts of interest, to immigration and the investigation into the late financier and convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

1789 Capital President Omeed Malik and Trump Jr. denied any wrongdoing at an Axios event last week.

"We responded to Congressman Raskin back in September pointing out in detail the many flaws in his understanding of how 1789 has operated and a number of basic factual errors," Bill Burck, an attorney representing 1789 Capital, said in a statement. "These are personal attacks untethered to actual evidence."

Juul said it intended "to cooperate with any Congressional effort to understand our company."

A representative for online gun retailer GrabAGun said: "Congressman Raskin's letter is a political document, and its allegations are baseless."

Representatives for Trump Jr., Polymarket and Hadrian Automation did not immediately return requests for comment.

In a move legal experts say will likely face challenges, President Donald Trump sought on Friday to curb cooperation between the private sector and Congress, ordering companies with federal contracts to alert the White House before sharing information with lawmakers, and to withhold material deemed confidential.

Under the US Constitution, Congress has oversight powers and authority to obtain information, including via subpoenas that the administration has sought to limit in scope.

RASKIN HIGHLIGHTS TIMING OF INVESTMENTS

Raskin's expanded investigation focuses on how the four companies "benefited, or stand to benefit," from Trump administration contracts, regulatory decisions or proposed rule changes, which Raskin said could point to conflicts of interest or other misconduct.

In his letter to Polymarket, Raskin said that the company had effectively been banned from the US and was also under federal investigation before Trump returned to office.

In July 2025, regulators closed that probe and approved Polymarket's acquisition of a US platform that paved the way for it to re-enter the US market. The following month, Polymarket disclosed that 1789 Capital had made a strategic investment, Raskin wrote. Reuters and other outlets reported at the time that the investment was worth tens of millions of dollars.

Reuters reported last month that the Commodity Futures Trading Commission has reopened its probe into Polymarket.

Raskin also said that in July 2025, months after 1789 Capital made a $5 million investment in Juul, authorities eased restrictions on sales of some Juul products, with more authorized earlier this year.

GrabAGun went public in 2025 after merging with a special-purpose acquisition company backed by Malik. In May 2026, the Trump administration proposed rules to make it easier to direct-ship guns to customers, Raskin also said.

The GrabAGun representative said the proposed rule changes were well known across the industry and that the company only provided input through the public comment process.

Raskin also wrote to Hadrian Automation, saying that the manufacturing company won US government contracts worth nearly $1 billion shortly after 1789 Capital acquired a stake in the company.

Raskin said that the president himself has publicly acknowledged the business conflicts, telling CNBC in July: "I feel badly in a way for my kids ... Almost anything they do ... they have inside information."

items.title: Salvadoran migrant Kilmar Abrego Garcia lands in Spain after US departure deal
items.content_html:
MADRID, Nov 25 (Reuters) - Salvadoran migrant Kilmar Abrego Garcia, whose wrongful deportation to El Salvador made him a focus for critics of President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown, arrived in Spain on Wednesday after leaving the US under a deal with the authorities.

Reuters witnesses saw Abrego Garcia, 31, who was wearing a Chicago Bulls cap and sunglasses, leave the airport building and board a car, without making any comment.

Abrego Garcia's arrival in Spain brings to a close a legal battle that reached the US Supreme Court after authorities deported him to a megaprison in El Salvador in March 2025 despite a court order barring his return there because of the risk of persecution.

His lawyer, Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, told reporters in Madrid his client's departure from the US, as a free man to the country of his choice on a commercial flight, was a victory because it was what he had been seeking since August 2025.

LAWYER SAYS MOVE TO SPAIN IS TEMPORARY

The lawyer has said the move to Spain is temporary and that Abrego Garcia could have legal avenues to return to the US under a future administration.

"We understand that under the Trump administration, he's never going to get a fair shake," the lawyer said.

"Kilmar Abrego Garcia is going to last a lot longer than Donald Trump, and he will be back in the United States as a lawful permanent resident under the next administration."

Spain has been a target of criticism by the Trump administration over the Socialist-led government's decision to regularise hundreds of thousands of illegal migrants. The criticism intensified after a mass crossing by over 80,000 migrants to its North African enclave of Ceuta in late July.

The US Department of Homeland Security said in a post on X Abrego Garcia had "self-deported" to Spain, adding that it was unsurprised by his choice of "a country that earlier this year was invaded by tens of thousands of illegal aliens".

"Spain's radical open-border policies have made the once-great country a breeding ground for illegal migrants," it said.

US officials had called Abrego Garcia's removal to El Salvador an "administrative error", but for months said they could not bring him back.

Ordered by the US Supreme Court to facilitate Abrego Garcia's return, the Trump administration ultimately brought him back to the US in June 2025. It later attempted to deport him to Liberia on a human smuggling charge that was dismissed by a US judge.

items.title: US finds no evidence China directed executive to spy on Nvidia CEO, WSJ reports
items.content_html:
Nov 25 (Reuters) - US officials found no evidence that tech executive Alice Huang was directed by Beijing to spy on Nvidia (NVDA.O) CEO Jensen Huang, the Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday, citing people familiar with a classified briefing.

The briefing comes after US President Donald Trump cleared the way for Jensen Huang's reinstatement earlier this week, assuring Nvidia that its CEO posed no national-security threat.

The controversy began with concerns over Alice Huang's alleged Chinese intelligence links and whether her relationship with Jensen Huang affected suspected diversions of Nvidia chips to China.

Officials from the CIA, FBI, Office of the Director of National Intelligence and National Security Agency briefed staff from congressional intelligence committees and chamber leaders, the Journal reported.

The officials said Alice Huang contacted China's spy agency during the affair but found no indication that she provided significant intelligence, the Journal reported.

Nvidia and the agencies did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment. Reuters could not independently verify the report.

Shares of Nvidia tumbled more than 7%, putting the chipmaker on track to shed more than $250 billion in market value and eroding a 31% comeback rally after CEO Huang's reinstatement that added over $900 billion.

The report said current evidence suggests that Alice Huang and Jensen Huang may have had an amorous relationship, but not a coordinated play by China, adding that new information could, however, change that assessment.

The briefing also noted that Kang Wei, described to the Journal as Alice Huang's husband by people who know them, was an asset for China's Ministry of State Security who remained in frequent contact with the intelligence service.

Reporting by Anhata Rooprai in Bengaluru; Editing by Shinjini Ganguli

items.title: US CIA, ODNI suffer cybersecurity breach of some unclassified information, source says
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 24 (Reuters) - The US Central Intelligence Agency and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence recently discovered a cybersecurity breach that exposed some of their unclassified information, according to a person familiar with the matter.

The intrusions affected a network that looks for intelligence insights in public, unclassified material, according to the New York Times, which first reported on the breach.

While it was not clear specifically what unclassified material was compromised, information at other government agencies was also believed to have been exposed in the breach, the Times added.

Asked about the report, the ODNI said there had been "no disruptions to critical capabilities or classified systems."

The news is the latest in a series of tech outages and cybersecurity incidents, including a breach reported at the US Department of Agriculture. Two separate breaches have recently been disclosed at the FBI, while the Pentagon and the Department of Homeland Security have also been caught up in recent cyber incidents.

The Times report did not say how the breach occurred.
