items.title: Radar issue delaying flights at Chicago O'Hare airport, FAA says
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 24 (Reuters) - An outage with a ground radar system is delaying flights into Chicago O'Hare International Airport and could force a halt to arriving flights, the US Federal Aviation Administration said on Tuesday.

The FAA said it "is temporarily delaying some flights while technicians work to repair a piece of air traffic equipment."

Air traffic control uses the ground surveillance radar and tracking system, known as ASDE-X, to monitor aircraft and vehicles on airport runways and taxiways. The FAA warned if the airport became congested, it could again temporarily halt arriving flights.

According to flight tracking website FlightAware, about 13%, or 373 flights, have been delayed at the American (AAL.O) and United Airlines (UAL.O) hub on what the FAA says is the busiest day for flights during the Thanksgiving holiday travel period.

The FAA, which earlier on Tuesday had paused most arriving flights into O'Hare, said delays were averaging 47 minutes and the issue could last until 1 a.m. ET (0600 GMT) on Wednesday. The FAA said some flights were being forced to hold for up to 30 minutes in the air before landing.

The FAA and airlines have faced a series of issues since a router outage triggered a nationwide ground stop on November 13 that lasted nearly five hours and led to more than 18,000 cancelled flights and affected more than 1.5 million passengers.

Reporting by David Shepardson and Jasper Ward in Washington, editing by Chris Reese, Rod Nickel and Lincoln Feast.

items.title: US third-quarter GDP growth revised sharply higher
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 25 (Reuters) - The US economy grew faster than initially thought in the third quarter, powered by robust consumer spending and business investment in artificial intelligence.

Gross domestic product increased at a 4.3% annualized rate last quarter, the fastest pace in three years, the Commerce Department's Bureau of Economic Analysis said in its second estimate of third-quarter GDP. The economy was previously estimated to have grown at a 3.4% pace.

Economists polled by Reuters had expected GDP growth would be revised up to a 3.5% pace. The economy grew at a 2.2% rate in the April-June quarter.

The revision reflected upgrades to consumer spending and business investment. Growth in consumer spending, which accounts for more than two-thirds of the economy, was revised up to a 4.2% rate from the previously reported 3.8% pace.

Spending is being mostly driven by higher-income households, whose wealth was boosted by the stock market, before the recent AI-led selloff. Historically low layoffs and moderate hiring are also helping other households to sustain spending, though wage gains have at times lagged inflation. Households are also saving less and dipping into their nest eggs.

Business spending on equipment increased at a 21.8% rate. That was an upgrade from the 20.9% rate of growth estimated last month. Business investment has posted three straight quarters of double-digit growth, but economists warned that the trend could slow as investors scrutinize AI valuations.

Final sales to private domestic purchasers, which exclude inventories, trade and government, accelerated at a 5.8% rate, the fastest since the second quarter of 2021. This measure of domestic demand, closely watched by policymakers, was previously estimated to have surged at a 4.9% rate.

Profits from current production increased at a rate of $206.0 billion last quarter after rising at a pace of $384.0 billion in the April-June quarter.

When measured from the income side, the economy grew at a 4.4% rate last quarter. Gross domestic income increased at a 2.3% pace in the second quarter. The average of GDP and GDI, considered a better measure of economic activity, grew at a 4.4% rate. Gross domestic output grew at a 2.2% rate in the April-June quarter.

Reporting by Lucia Mutikani; Editing by Paul Simao

items.title: US weekly jobless claims fall more than expected
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 25 (Reuters) - The number of Americans filing new claims for unemployment benefits fell more than expected last week, pointing to stable labor market conditions.

Initial claims for state unemployment benefits dropped 13,000 to a seasonally adjusted 189,000 for the week ended November 21, the Labor Department said on Wednesday. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast 200,000 claims for the latest week. The report was published a day early because of Thursday's Thanksgiving holiday. Claims have been running considerably low since mid-July. Economists still view the labor market as being in a "low-hire, low-fire" state of full employment.

The number of people receiving unemployment benefits after an initial week of aid, a proxy for hiring, tumbled 95,000 to a seasonally adjusted 1.697 million during the week ended November 14. The so-called continuing claims covered the period during which the government surveyed households for November's unemployment rate.

The Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago is forecasting the unemployment rate ticking up to 4.16%, which would round up to 4.2% from 4.14% in October. The jobless rate dropped from 4.5% in November last year to 4.1% in October, though part of the decrease has been due to a smaller labor force amid retirements and the Trump administration's immigration crackdown.

The outlook for the labor market received a boost from a Conference Board survey on Tuesday showing the share of consumers saying jobs were "plentiful" soared in November to its highest level since May 2025, while the proportion viewing jobs as "hard to get" was the lowest in just over a year.

A stable labor market likely clears the way for the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates again beyond December's anticipated hike as it tries to bring inflation under control.

Reporting by Lucia Mutikani; Editing by Chizu Nomiyama

items.title: Nidal Hasan asks US judge for stay of execution for Fort Hood murders
items.content_html:
Nov 24 (Reuters) - (This Nov 24 story has been corrected to say military police shot Hasan, not that he shot himself, in paragraph 7.)

Nidal Hasan, the former US Army major sentenced to be executed next week at the same Fort Hood military base where he murdered 13 people in 2009, asked a federal judge on Tuesday to halt the execution while he mounts a legal challenge to his sentence.

President Donald Trump in October approved the firing squad execution of Hasan, calling him "a very bad and evil man," while Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth made the unprecedented promise to livestream Hasan's death at the Texas military base. Trump scrapped Hegseth's broadcast plans after widespread outcry.

Hasan, imprisoned at the Fort Leavenworth military base in Kansas, has asked a federal judge in Topeka to issue a stay of execution, potentially delaying it by months or years.

US District Judge Anthony Mattivi ordered a hearing about the stay scheduled for Wednesday morning.

Under US law, a condemned person can seek legal review of their detention and sentence, known as a habeas corpus petition, once they have been told the date and method of their execution.

A spokesperson for the Department of Defense did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist, used a laser-sighted handgun to kill 13 people in a medical facility at the sprawling Fort Hood base before military police ended the attack by shooting him. Hasan was paralyzed from the chest down and later convicted of 13 counts of premeditated murder by a military court-martial jury in 2013.

The US military has not carried out an execution following a court-martial conviction since 1961, and Hasan would become the first person the US military has executed by firing squad since 1945.

Of the four men on the US military's death row, only one besides Hasan has had an execution approved and scheduled by a US president: Ronald Gray was scheduled to be executed in December 2008, but his execution was indefinitely stayed by a judge through the same habeas petition Hasan is using this week.

Hasan, born in the US to Palestinian parents, represented himself at his military trial. The judge did not allow him to pursue his planned defense that the killings were justified because he was defending the Taliban in Afghanistan from the US military.

In his petition, Hasan said he intends to argue that being barred from advancing this defense at his trial was a violation of his constitutional rights to due process, and that Trump and Hegseth violated military rules when setting Hasan's execution date, including by promising to broadcast his death.

The motion for a stay of execution filed by lawyers from the American Civil Liberties Union of Kansas said that Hasan again intends to represent himself in the habeas proceedings, where a judge will decide if his conviction and sentence were constitutional.

"There is no question that the violence committed at Fort Hood caused unimaginable pain and loss," Anna Arceneaux, deputy director of the ACLU's Capital Punishment Project, said in a statement. "But the gravity of that loss does not change the government's obligation to uphold the principles that define our justice system."

Reporting by Jonathan Allen in New York, Phil Stewart and Kanishka Singh in Washington; Editing by Stephen Coates and Cynthia Osterman

items.title: Trump set to add new sweeping tariffs, undeterred by midterms defeat
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 25 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump is set to reignite global trade tensions with new tariffs on major trading partners, sources said, undeterred in his protectionist push by major losses by his Republican Party in US midterm elections.

The Trump administration's announcement, expected imminently, will address what it has argued is excess industrial capacity in 16 major US trading partners, three people with knowledge of the matter said on Tuesday.

They include China, which is poised to rack up a record trade surplus of well over $1 trillion in 2026, though the tariff level is expected to remain within the range agreed under the current truce between Trump and his counterpart Xi Jinping.

The prospect of new US tariffs was a further factor weighing on global stock markets on Wednesday as a tech-led rally continued to run out of steam, with Nasdaq futures down over 2%.

"It is another reminder that while the legal justification for tariffs keeps changing, US protectionism is becoming increasingly difficult to unwind," ING analysts wrote in a note.

On Wednesday, Beijing reiterated its opposition to "trade wars" and once again dismissed the notion of overcapacity, but stopped short of threatening retaliation.

"The so-called 'overcapacity' is a false issue, and China opposes using it as an excuse for political manipulation," foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said.

"Both China and the United States should jointly implement the important consensus reached by their heads of state and maintain the stable development of bilateral economic and trade relations," Guo said.

TARIFF WALL

Analysts say, however, higher US trade barriers against China and other economies are the direction of travel, even if the Democratic Party — which won majorities in both houses of Congress earlier this month — tried to curb Trump's tariff impulses.

The tariffs have in part contributed to higher prices on consumer goods in the US, a major source of discontent among voters.

"Without the two-thirds majority needed to override a presidential veto, Democrats' ability to dismantle the tariff wall will remain limited," ING analysts said in a note.

"Either way, we don't think the blue wave will mark a return to free trade. The Biden years already showed that tariffs in strategically important sectors enjoy support across political camps."

The US-China truce runs until January 10, but many expect it to be extended — potentially as early as next month when Trump and Xi are set to meet again at a G20 gathering in Miami — given the major impact a re-escalation of tit-for-tat hikes similar to those seen in 2025 would have on both economies.

The agreement caps Trump's second-term tariffs on Chinese goods at 20%, in addition to duties of about 25% imposed during his first term. The US has already imposed a 12.5% anti-forced labor duty on all Chinese imports, leaving only 7.5% to reach the 20% cap.

The US and China also are working to cut tariffs on $30 billion of non-strategic imports from each side.

TAILORED RATES

One of the people said that the duties would be specifically tailored to each country, with goods from Mexico and Norway unlikely to see any immediate levies.

The White House is expected to honor capped tariff rates that were included in finalized US trade deals with partner countries, this person said. These include duty ceilings of 15% on goods from the EU, Japan and South Korea and 19% for Malaysia.

The US also is expected to honor the 20% cap on Trump's second-term tariffs on goods from China, as long as a trade truce with Beijing is extended. If it expires, the Chinese excess capacity rate would rise to a higher level.

The USTR and the White House did not respond to Reuters queries about the pending announcement.

REPLACEMENT TARIFFS

The trading partners included in the probe are China, India, Japan, South Korea, Mexico, Vietnam, Taiwan, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia, Switzerland, Norway, Singapore, Bangladesh and Cambodia, along with the European Union.

USTR launched the excess capacity probe in March, under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, along with a separate investigation into weak or lax enforcement of anti-forced labor laws in 59 countries and the European Union. Together, the duties are meant to rebuild Trump's global "Liberation Day" tariffs that were struck down by the US Supreme Court in February.

The Trump administration has singled out China as the biggest source of excess industrial capacity, which it says is flooding global markets with steel, aluminum, electric vehicles, appliances, solar products and other goods. China says its exports reflect competitive advantages.

The probe is also partly directed at Chinese investment in Southeast Asian countries, including Vietnam, Indonesia and Cambodia, to manufacture goods for the US market and avoid prior US tariffs.

items.title: East Coast storm to bring rain, strong winds on US Thanksgiving
items.content_html:
NEW YORK, Nov 24 (Reuters) - Storms bringing heavy rain and winds up and down the Eastern Seaboard are threatening to delay flights during one of the busiest travel weeks of the year and could ground some of the biggest balloons in the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, forecasters said on Tuesday.

Rainfall rates could reach 1 inch (2.5 cm) per hour at times, with wind gusts exceeding 50 mph (80 kph), according to the National Weather Service.

Onshore winds, king tides — the highest high-tide cycles of the year — and this week's full moon could combine to produce moderate to major coastal flooding from Georgia and the Carolinas to Long Island. At least minor coastal flooding is also forecast across coastal New England.

The National Weather Service issued a coastal flood warning for the San Francisco Bay Area through late Thursday afternoon, warning that flooding could reach 2.7 feet (0.8 meter) in some low-lying areas as near-record high tides swell the region's waterways.

Rain is expected to spread across much of the Southeast on Wednesday, potentially disrupting Thanksgiving travel for millions of Americans, before advancing into the Mid-Atlantic and Ohio Valley by Wednesday night. Washington state and coastal Oregon are also forecast to see rain, with snow in the mountains.

In New York City, home to the 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, conditions are expected to remain dry for the 8:30 a.m. ET (1330 GMT) start. Rain is forecast to develop by late morning or early afternoon and intensify through the evening. City rules require parade balloons to fly at lower elevations or remain grounded if sustained winds exceed 23 mph or gusts top 34 mph.

The Federal Aviation Administration expects the busiest Thanksgiving travel period in 16 years, with more than 417,000 flights scheduled during the nine-day window. Tuesday is forecast to be the busiest day, with 52,000 flights. The agency said in a press release that rain could affect flights across the Southeast, including Atlanta, on Wednesday before moving into the Mid-Atlantic later in the day.

Reporting by Helen Coster; editing by Donna Bryson and Aurora Ellis

items.title: Wisconsin reports third measles-related death this year
items.content_html:
Nov 25 (Reuters) - Wisconsin reported a third measles-related death on Tuesday, as the United States grapples with its worst outbreak of the viral infection in decades.

The latest death involved an adult resident of Lafayette County, the state's health department said. Wisconsin has reported 918 cases and 19 hospitalizations across 24 counties since August.

An HHS spokesperson said the agency was "saddened to hear of a death in Wisconsin" and that the CDC is working with state and local officials through its Epi-Aid emergency response program to curb further spread.

Earlier this month, Wisconsin reported two measles-associated deaths, involving an infant and a child from Grant County.

"This is terrible news for the nation and clear evidence that reduced vaccination rates are enabling measles to get a foothold in communities across the country," said Frederic Bertley, immunologist and CEO of the Center of Science and Industry.

The US is grappling with its largest measles outbreak in more than three decades, a resurgence driven largely by unvaccinated people that this month stripped the country of its hard-fought measles elimination status.

The country has reported 5,838 confirmed measles cases and six associated deaths in 2026, according to data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

However, based on publicly reported state figures, the US has recorded at least 14 measles-associated deaths this year, including nine fatalities in Pennsylvania and one each in Virginia and New York state.

A discrepancy between state and federal death tallies arose earlier this year after CDC, under US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., began using National Center for Health Statistics mortality data instead of state figures.

The agency has said it is working with the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists to develop a standardized case definition for measles deaths.

items.title: Thomas Markle charged in US on second count of possessing child sexual abuse material
items.content_html:
LOS ANGELES, Nov 24 (Reuters) - Thomas Markle, the estranged father of Britain's Duchess of Sussex, Meghan Markle, and father-in-law of Britain's Prince Harry, was indicted on Tuesday in US federal court on two counts of possessing child sexual abuse material.

The indictment doubles the number of federal charges currently lodged in Los Angeles against the 82-year-old Markle in a case that grew out of an investigation initiated last month in the Philippines, where he previously resided.

The elder Markle was originally charged on November 5 in a criminal complaint with a single felony count of possessing child sexual abuse images.

According to an FBI affidavit filed with the complaint, the material in question was found in two Los Angeles storage units and included two explicit photos of Markle posed with a naked underage girl and other images of him with children in various stages of undress.

One of the photos showed a naked girl in a room that appeared to be part of a motel chain in the Philippines, the affidavit said.

Philippine police said last week criminal complaints had been filed against Markle in the country's Cebu province, where he once lived, accusing him of violating local laws against online sexual abuse and exploitation of children.

Markle has denied the allegations, telling the Daily Mail the claims were untrue and describing them as "sick lies."

He was arrested on November 6 at a Florida assisted-living facility where he has been a patient, and is expected to be transferred to California in the coming weeks to be arraigned in US District Court in Los Angeles on the two-count grand jury indictment returned on Tuesday.

Following a court-ordered psychiatric evaluation of Markle, a US magistrate judge in Tampa, Florida, last week ruled that he was mentally competent to stand trial, meaning that he understood the proceedings against him and could assist in his own defense.

Each count of possession of child sexual abuse material, an offense referred to in the US criminal code as possession of child pornography, is punishable by up to 20 years in prison if he is convicted, the US attorney's statement said.

Meghan Markle, an American actor, has been estranged from her father since the run-up to her marriage to King Charles' younger son, Harry, in 2018, when the duchess has said she first became aware of allegations against her father. She has said she was "deeply distressed" over the matter, which led her to cut off contact between her father and her two children, Archie, 7, and Lilibet, 5.

Reporting by Steve Gorman in Los Angeles; Editing by Chris Reese and Lincoln Feast.

items.title: Trump spares turkeys Freedom and Feathers from fowl Thanksgiving fate
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 24 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump has described the presidential pardon as "extreme powers." On Tuesday, he used it to spare two turkeys from the imminent threat of becoming Thanksgiving dinner.

Trump granted pardons to Freedom and Feathers, the 4-month-old fowl selected for the annual White House ritual.

Raised at Deans Gap Farm in Fort Seybert, West Virginia, the birds spent Monday night at the lavish Willard InterContinental Hotel in Washington before their White House appearance. Trump said next year's turkeys could stay overnight in the new White House state ballroom, where he said he would also hold the pardon ceremony.

Online voters selected Freedom to receive Trump's formal pardon, but both birds will retire to Texas A&M University after their reprieve.

At Tuesday's ceremony on the White House's new South Lawn helipad, Trump gazed at Freedom and noticed his companion was missing.

"Where's Feathers?" he asked.

The second turkey was resting in the White House, officials said. Trump quipped that he'd run off into the bushes.

Moments later, he rested his hand on the bird's fluffy white plumes.

"Freedom," Trump said, "I just want to say, that you and Feathers, as of this moment, have a complete and total pardon."

The tradition dates back more than a century, when poultry farmers sent turkeys to the White House as holiday gifts, forcing presidents and first ladies to coordinate avian logistics to handle the incoming birds — many of which arrived alive. In 1989, President George H.W. Bush formalized a reprieve for the birds, turning the annual turkey presentation into a pardon.

The rising cost of a Thanksgiving dinner could cast a shadow this year on Americans' turkey-centered feasts.

Holiday staples are 6% more expensive this year than 2025, according to the American Farm Bureau Federation. Turkey prices jumped more than 10%, according to the federation, which cited Department of Agriculture data on strong demand, including for exports, and low inventories.

Consumer prices for other Thanksgiving staples and ingredients, such as ham, milk, dinner rolls, sweet potatoes and cranberries, also increased.

Earlier on Tuesday, Trump awarded the Medal of Freedom, the nation's highest civilian honor, to Rudy Giuliani, his one-time personal attorney and New York mayor during the September 11, 2001, attacks on the World Trade Center buildings.

Giuliani himself was once the beneficiary of a Trump reprieve. Trump pardoned Giuliani in 2025 as he faced legal fallout for attempting to overturn the 2020 election results.
